description:
The declared intake lexicon. This file is DATA, deliberately not code: the ruling on each discretionary phrase must be reviewable by a human without reading Python. Every entry is governed by docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, which states the boundary this file applies: PARAMETERISE a term whose measurement basis is known but whose threshold is unset; REFUSE a term whose measurement basis is itself undefined. Anything not declared here refuses (see unknown_term_policy). A ruled term is also only ruled for the LITERAL parts of its pattern: term_match_policy states that a term's declared basis_slot is a wildcard and not ruled text, so a REFUSE term or a discretionary marker sitting in it still surfaces, and that no term match may span a sentence boundary. A ruled term is also only ruled for the claim its pattern declares: basis_qualifiers lists the constructions that re-base a term onto a different measurement, and basis_qualifier_policy states what happens when one is found ATTACHED to the ruled measurement inside the declared window (a REFUSE, like any undeclared term), which attachments count (basis_qualifier_policy.attachment), and what that check cannot see (basis_qualifier_policy.limits). Patterns are Python regular expressions matched against the source text after lowercasing and whitespace collapsing.

Every PARAMETERISE term declares realised_by: the catalogue entry and parameter that its declared parameter is actually implemented as. Intake and the catalogue are two halves of one ruling, and the link between them is DECLARED here rather than left to matching names — the names deliberately do not match. tests/test_lexicon_catalogue_agreement.py fails if a link points at a catalogue entry or parameter that does not exist, or if the two sides disagree on type, units, default or allowed_range. A PARAMETERISE term also declares hermes_basis_relationship, which states how the basis fields intake declares are derived from the fields the catalogue entry actually consumes.

unknown_term_policy.why_unresolved_template: The phrase "{phrase}" is discretionary language ({marker_reason}) that has no entry in HSA's declared intake lexicon (hsa/intake/lexicon.json). HSA therefore has no ratified measurement basis for it and cannot establish one without inventing trading semantics the source never stated. Unknown discretionary terms fail closed by policy rather than passing through unflagged, because an unflagged term becomes an assumption baked into a governed strategy (PID line 39; docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'Unknown terms fail closed').

resolution_needed.description_template: State what "{phrase}" measures: the quantity to compute and the HERMES facts to compute it from. If a settled measurement basis exists, add it to hsa/intake/lexicon.json with a ruling under docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md so future intakes resolve it consistently.

term_match_policy.description: How much of a term match is actually RULED text, and where a match may end. A term's pattern is part literal and part wildcard: the literal parts are the phrase the lexicon rules on, and the declared basis_slot group is a wildcard run of words that merely sits between them. Treating the whole matched span as ruled is what let a slot swallow "near resistance" — a PID line 115 must-not-guess phrase — and hide it, because anything a ruled term consumed was never scanned again. This block states the three rules that close that, and all three are enforced for EVERY term, not for the terms that happened to expose the bug. overlap_resolution is the general one the other two turned out to be special cases of: suppression requires a ruling that COVERS the text end to end, and a PARAMETERISE term whose match collides with unresolved language anywhere — wildcard slot or literal head noun — does not resolve.

sentence_boundary.intra_token_exception: A terminator character with a word character on BOTH sides is inside a token, not between two sentences, so "1.5", "m.a", "h.4", "4.hour", "vwap.session" and "a.m" are each one token. "trade. some" still ends a sentence (a space follows), so does "the range." at the end of the text, and so does "the range.)" before a bracket. This was declared as a DECIMAL exception — a '.' between two DIGITS — and that narrowness is where the fifth audit's defect entered: every dotted abbreviation that VIDEO_DERIVED and TRADER_EXPLANATION intake actually carries (PID lines 104-105) was read as a mid-word sentence ending, and a term match spanning one was judged to cross a boundary. The decimal case is the special case of this rule, not the rule. Only '.' takes the exception: it is the only terminator with an intra-token job in trading prose and the only one a declared basis_slot may consume.
sentence_boundary.precedence: A recognised term match that crosses a sentence boundary does NOT resolve and is NOT accepted as a ruling — it suppresses nothing, so every other term and every marker still scans the far side of the boundary freely, which is the concern that originally justified discarding it. It is reported all the same. HSA recognised the words; it cannot read them as that term; and telling the reader neither of those things is the silent guess PID line 39 forbids. Same disposition, same severity and same fail-closed direction as unruled_slot_content and overlap_resolution, because it is the same condition: a recognised term the analyser will not resolve.
sentence_boundary.why: A term match may not span a sentence boundary. A ruled phrase is a phrase, and "a large trade. some wick setups only" is not one — it is the tail of one sentence and the head of the next, joined only because a wildcard slot tolerated a token ending in a full stop. Enforced on the MATCH, in the analyser, rather than left to each pattern's character classes: a pattern-by-pattern fix holds only until the next pattern is written, and this rule holds for a term nobody has declared yet. The patterns are also tightened so their slots cannot consume a terminator in the first place, which is belt and braces, not the guarantee. What this rule may NOT do is delete the match. Not accepting it and not reporting it are two separate decisions, and only the first was ever justified: for four audits this was a bare discard, so a recognised term crossing a boundary produced no finding of any kind and the source drafted at exit 0 claiming nothing recognised had survived unruled. The match is now refused AND reported, exactly like the other two rules in this block.
sentence_boundary.why_unresolved_template: HSA's declared pattern for the ruled term "{term_label}" matched across a sentence boundary here: "{context_text}". A ruled term is a phrase and a phrase does not straddle a sentence terminator ({terminators}), so HSA will not read this as "{term_label}" — and it will not tell you the source is clean either, because it recognised the words. Either the source says "{term_label}" and the boundary in the middle of it is a typo, or it says two different things either side of the boundary and one of them has been left undefined. Guessing which is what PID line 39 forbids (docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'A term match may not span a sentence boundary').

resolution_needed.description_template: Restate "{context_text}" so no ruled phrase runs across the sentence terminator. If "{term_label}" was meant as one phrase, remove the boundary inside it; if two separate statements were meant, say each one in full so HSA rules on each separately.

slot_is_not_ruled_text.rule: The words a term's declared basis_slot consumed are NOT part of the ruled phrase. Only the literal parts of the match — the span minus the slot — suppress further scanning. Every other ruled term and every discretionary marker is matched against slot contents exactly as if the slot were ordinary prose, because that is what it is.
slot_is_not_ruled_text.why: The suppression rule was justified as "text inside the match is part of the ruled phrase the lexicon declares". For the literal parts that is true. For the wildcard slot it is false, and the consequence was silent: "a large near resistance wick" resolved at exit 0 with no refusal and no advisory, because near_resistance and the proximity marker both fell inside a span the analyser had already written off as ruled. basis_qualifier_policy.attachment already treats the slot as scannable for re-basings (attachment form SLOT); this states the same thing for the other two things that can be in there.

unruled_slot_content.precedence: A PARAMETERISE term whose slot contains a REFUSE term or an unruled discretionary marker does NOT resolve. The slot modifies the measurement, so undefined language sitting in it is undefined language about the measurement; resolving the term anyway would declare a parameter for a quantity the source has not finished describing. Refusing here is the same fail-closed direction the rest of this file takes.
unruled_slot_content.why_unresolved_template: HSA recognised the ruled term "{term_label}" here, but the words its pattern tolerates between its ruled adjective and its ruled head noun — "{slot_text}" — are themselves unresolved: {findings}. Those words modify the measurement, so the ruled basis for "{term_label}" ({measurement_basis}) does not describe what the source asked for. The slot is a wildcard and is not ruled text; language inside it fails closed exactly as it would anywhere else in the source (PID line 39; docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'A wildcard slot is not ruled text').

resolution_needed.description_template: Resolve the unresolved language inside "{phrase}" first: {findings}. Then restate the rule so "{term_label}" is either qualified by measured words or left unqualified, in which case its ratified basis ({measurement_basis}) applies.

overlap_resolution.rule: Overlap resolution decides which term PARAMETERISES. It never decides that a recognised term or marker was not said. A match is treated as already ruled on, and dropped, only when the accepted rulings COVER it end to end; a match that merely overlaps one is kept and reported. A PARAMETERISE term whose own matched span — its literal head nouns included, not the wildcard slot alone — overlaps a REFUSE term, an unruled discretionary marker, or a second ruled term does NOT resolve.
overlap_resolution.precedence: REFUSE wins outright. Where a ruled PARAMETERISE phrase and a ruled REFUSE phrase claim the same words, the source has written two readings over the top of one another, and which one it means is exactly what is undefined. Both are reported: the refusal on its own terms, and the PARAMETERISE term as a contested match that does not resolve. The same holds when both rulings are PARAMETERISE — "a large no-wick candle" is large_wick and no_wick_candle claiming one phrase between them, and declaring the threshold the analyser sorted first would put a number on a contradiction the source has not settled.
overlap_resolution.why: The contest is ordered leftmost, then longest, then lexicon order, and for three audits the loser was simply discarded. Discarding is safe between two PARAMETERISE readings and silent for a refusal: "no-wick close to resistance" gives the ruled word "close" to no_wick_candle, so near_resistance — a PID line 115 must-not-guess phrase — lost the contest, was dropped, and the source resolved at exit 0 with nothing unresolved at all. Scoping the earlier repairs to the wildcard slot fixed the phrasings that used the slot and left every phrasing that collides with a literal head noun. This rule is stated over the MATCH, in the analyser, so it holds for a term nobody has declared yet rather than for the patterns written so far.
overlap_resolution.why_unresolved_template: HSA recognised the ruled term "{term_label}" here, but its ruled phrase overlaps language the lexicon does not resolve: {findings}. The colliding text is "{context_text}". Two rulings claim the same words, so the ratified basis for "{term_label}" ({measurement_basis}) may not be what the source is describing at all. Settling that by which match the analyser happened to sort first would be a silent guess (PID line 39; docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'Overlap resolution never deletes a refusal').

resolution_needed.description_template: Restate "{context_text}" so the two readings are separated: {findings}. Say which condition the rule actually depends on, and give the unresolved one a measurable definition. If "{term_label}" was meant on its own, its ratified basis ({measurement_basis}) applies once the collision is gone.

discretionary_markers.reason: a quality judgement with no stated measure
a clarity judgement with no stated measure
a health judgement with no stated measure
a proximity claim with no stated tolerance
an approximation with no stated tolerance
a significance claim with no stated threshold
a sufficiency claim with no stated threshold
a hedged rule that never states when it applies
an importance claim with no stated construction

window.description: The outer bound on where a qualifier may be looked for: the sentence the matched term sits in, plus sentences_after sentences following it. Sentences are split on the terminators above, over the lowercased whitespace-collapsed text. The window BOUNDS the search; it does not decide the outcome — attachment does (see basis_qualifier_policy.attachment). Being inside the window is necessary and NOT sufficient: a qualifier merely co-occurring here does not re-base anything. In practice sentences_after governs the GLOSS form alone, because SLOT and COMPLEMENT attachment cannot cross a sentence terminator; sentences_after 1 reaches the trailing gloss ("...a large wick. By large I mean twice the ATR.") and 0 does not. tests/test_ambiguity.py exercises that difference directly, so this number is a declared tunable with observable behaviour rather than an unread constant.

attachment.rule: A declared qualifier re-bases a ruled term ONLY when it is syntactically attached to the ruled measurement — modifying the term itself, or standing as the term's own comparative complement, or glossing the term's own word. A qualifier that merely co-occurs in the window attaches to something else in the sentence and is NOT a re-basing. This is a deliberate choice of PRECISION over RECALL, and the reason it is safe is that it is not the only thing telling the truth: every resolution this guard permits still carries source_basis_agreement NOT_VERIFIED, which declines to certify that the source agrees with the ruled basis. A guard that fired on every co-occurrence would refuse ordinary trading prose — an ATR stop, a bar-count expiry, a moving-average trend filter — and refusing a valid strategy is a defect, not caution. See docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'What attaches a qualifier to a ruled term'.

forms.description: The qualifier overlaps the term's own modifier slot: the basis_slot group each PARAMETERISE pattern declares, which is the run of words the pattern allows between its ruled adjective and its ruled head noun. Words sitting in that slot modify the measurement itself, so any category attaches there — "a large ATR wick", "a large recent wick", "a larger than average wick". This form is why a hit INSIDE a term's matched span must be examined rather than discarded: the slot is a wildcard, and a re-basing lands in it.

A COMPARATIVE qualifier begins immediately after the term match, with nothing between them but complement_filler. A comparative is the connective that binds a yardstick to a measurement, which is what makes it attach: "a large wick RELATIVE TO the recent average". Non-comparative qualifiers never attach this way, because a bare yardstick noun after the term attaches to whatever else the clause is about — "a large wick above the 200 period moving average" places the wick, it does not measure it. Once a comparative has attached, qualifiers of any category lying between it and the end of its sentence name the displacing basis and are reported with it.

The source restates the term's own ruled word and then defines it: "a large wick, and by large I mean twice the 14-period ATR". What attaches the gloss is that it NAMES one of the words the term itself matched — gloss_constructions carry an {anchor} placeholder which is replaced, per match, by the ruled words that match actually consumed. Qualifiers lying between the gloss and the end of its sentence are the basis the gloss states. A gloss naming no declared qualifier re-bases nothing. This is the only form that reaches past the term's own sentence, and how far it reaches is window.sentences_after.

gloss_constructions.reason: the source names the ruled word and then says what it means by it
the source defines the ruled word outright
the source defines or measures the ruled word as something

attachment.not_attached: Deliberately NOT treated as re-basing, because each attaches to something other than the ruled measurement: a stop or target sized in ATR ("a large wick. My stop is 2 ATR below entry."); a bar-count expiry or persistence window, which PID line 137 REQUIRES a package to state ("the setup expires within 3 bars", "expires after 4 bars"); a trend or location filter naming an average ("a large wick above the 200 period moving average"); a reference to prior bars used as a price level rather than a yardstick ("a large wick that clears the previous bars' high"). These resolve, and source_basis_agreement stays NOT_VERIFIED.

basis_qualifier_policy.why_unresolved_template: HSA recognised the ruled term "{term_label}" here, but the text around it re-bases the measurement: {qualifiers}. The ratified basis for "{term_label}" is: {measurement_basis} docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md rules on the phrase the lexicon declares, and anything that changes the basis is a different term. An undeclared term refuses rather than being resolved onto a basis the source did not state, because applying the ruled basis here would make HSA assert a measurement the source itself displaced (PID line 39; docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'A ruled term can be re-based by its context').

resolution_needed.description_template: State which measurement basis governs "{phrase}": the ratified basis for "{term_label}" ({measurement_basis}) or the one the surrounding text names with {qualifier_phrases}. If the source's basis is a settled one, declare it in hsa/intake/lexicon.json as its own ruled term under docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md so future intakes resolve it consistently. If the ratified basis was what the source meant, restate the source without the re-basing language.

basis_qualifier_policy.limits: This is a declared surface-pattern check, not comprehension. It fires only on the constructions listed in basis_qualifiers, only inside the declared window, only for PARAMETERISE terms, and only when one of the attachment forms above actually holds. It is tuned for PRECISION, so it misses on purpose as well as by accident. Known misses, stated rather than implied: a re-basing worded outside the declared vocabulary; a re-basing attached by a connective the COMPLEMENT form does not list; a gloss phrased outside gloss_constructions; a gloss further away than window.sentences_after; a re-basing that modifies the term from the LEFT ("an ATR-relative large wick"); and a yardstick that genuinely governs the term but reads, on the surface, exactly like the location and expiry prose under not_attached. A term that survives this check is therefore NOT proven to carry the ruled basis — it is only a term in which no ATTACHED declared re-basing was found, which is why every resolution reports source_basis_agreement NOT_VERIFIED, names the declared qualifiers it saw and deliberately left unattached, and claims nothing more (docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'A ruled term can be re-based by its context').

basis_qualifiers.reason: an explicit comparison construction, which states the ruling against something other than the term's own declared basis
basis_qualifiers.pattern: \b(?:relative to|compared (?:to|with)|in comparison (?:to|with)|measured against|benchmarked against|in relation to|normalised by|normalized by|scaled by|as a (?:multiple|fraction|percentage|percent|proportion|share) of)\b

basis_qualifiers.reason: a comparison against a named measurement reference
an average or central-tendency reference, which needs a lookback the single-bar basis does not have
a rolling statistic over previous bars
an appeal to recent history, which is a lookback and not a property of the evaluated bar
an explicit lookback window over earlier bars
a volatility measure named as the yardstick instead of the term's declared basis
a statistical dispersion measure named as the yardstick
a multiplier applied to some other quantity, which makes that quantity the basis
an absolute price unit, which is a different basis from a ratio measured on the bar
basis_qualifiers.pattern: \b(?:in pips|in points|in ticks|in dollars|in absolute (?:price )?terms|absolute price terms)\b

basis_qualifiers.reason: other bars offered as the reference, which the single-bar basis does not read

terms.label: large wick
terms.pid_reference: PID line 114; required by acceptance Example B, PID line 242
terms.measurement_basis: Wick length as a fraction of the total bar range (candle.high minus candle.low) of the evaluated bar, measured on that one bar.
terms.basis_rationale: Both quantities are unambiguous single-bar HERMES facts. No level must be constructed, no lookback chosen, and no competing construction of 'wick' exists that would rank real bars differently. Only the cut-off is missing, and a cut-off is a bounded parameter (PID line 140), not a trading decision.

parameters.name: min_wick_to_range_ratio
parameters.description: Minimum ratio of wick length to the total bar range for the wick to count as large. Resolves the discretionary phrase 'large wick' onto its ratified measurement basis; the DEFAULT is provisional and must be settled by CER evidence before promotion (docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'Attribution').

realised_by.why_the_names_differ: Intake names a parameter after the phrase it resolves; the catalogue names it after the quantity and the comparator. Both conventions are already in force across their own files, so this link records the correspondence instead of renaming either side — a rename would change a promoted catalogue identity, which docs/VERSIONING.md forbids in place.
realised_by.range_reconciliation: Intake previously declared 0.3-0.9 with a 0.05 step while the realisation accepted 0.3-0.95 with no step. The catalogue bound is now declared on both sides. The catalogue is the side that actually runs and the side whose bound is reasoned about alongside body_to_range_ratio_max and opposing_wick_to_range_ratio_max, which is what makes a 0.95 ceiling coherent rather than degenerate; neither bound carries evidence, so the narrower one was an unratified extra restriction on the ruled basis rather than a safeguard. The step was dropped for the same reason: the realisation enforces no grid, so intake must not claim one.

hermes_basis_relationship.statement: Intake declares the BASIS fields — the quantities the ruling is stated in. The catalogue entry declares the DERIVATION fields — the raw HERMES facts those quantities are computed from. The two lists are deliberately different and must stay reconcilable: every basis field below is derived from fields the linked catalogue entry consumes, and every field the catalogue entry consumes is either used by a derivation or declared as catalogue-only with a reason.

catalogue_only_fields.why: The catalogue entry adds a minimum bar range as an ATR multiple (min_range_atr_multiple) so the ratio is not read off a bar too compressed to carry it. That guard is the realisation's, not the ruling's: docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md ratifies the wick-over-range basis only. A realisation may add a guard on top of the basis; it may not change the basis.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Upper wick length of the evaluated bar: high minus the greater of open and close.
Lower wick length of the evaluated bar: the lesser of open and close, minus low.
Total range of the evaluated bar: high minus low. Denominator of the wick ratio.

terms.label: no-wick candle
terms.pid_reference: PID line 55 names no-wick candle as an atomic example; required by acceptance Example B, PID line 242
terms.measurement_basis: The larger of the two wicks as a fraction of the total bar range (candle.high minus candle.low) of the evaluated bar, required to be at or below a declared cap, measured on that one bar.
terms.basis_rationale: The same single-bar basis as large_wick, read in the opposite direction. 'No wick' cannot mean exactly zero on real data, so a tolerance is unavoidable; that tolerance is a bounded parameter rather than a choice between constructions.

parameters.name: max_wick_to_range_ratio
parameters.description: Maximum ratio of the larger wick to the total bar range for the candle to count as no-wick. Resolves the discretionary tolerance in 'no-wick'; the DEFAULT is provisional and must be settled by CER evidence before promotion (docs/AMBIGUITY-POLICY.md, 'Attribution').

realised_by.why_the_names_differ: The same naming conventions as large_wick: intake names the phrase it resolves, the catalogue names the quantity and the comparator.
realised_by.range_reconciliation: Intake previously declared 0.0-0.25 with a 0.01 step while the realisation accepted 0.0-0.3 with no step. The catalogue bound is now declared on both sides. A 0.3 cap on either wick is only loose in isolation: the realisation bounds the same bar with body_to_range_ratio_min, whose own floor is 0.5, so the wider wick cap cannot on its own admit a bar with no body. Intake declares no body parameter, so its tighter cap was standing in for a constraint the realisation already carries elsewhere, and duplicating that constraint in a narrower bound made the two files disagree without making the strategy stricter. The step was dropped because the realisation enforces no grid.

hermes_basis_relationship.statement: Intake declares the BASIS fields — the quantities the ruling is stated in. The catalogue entry declares the DERIVATION fields — the raw HERMES facts those quantities are computed from. The two lists are deliberately different and must stay reconcilable: every basis field below is derived from fields the linked catalogue entry consumes, and every field the catalogue entry consumes is either used by a derivation or declared as catalogue-only with a reason.

catalogue_only_fields.why: The catalogue entry adds a minimum bar range as an ATR multiple (min_range_atr_multiple), and bounds the body with body_to_range_ratio_min. Both are the realisation's guards on top of the ruled wick-over-range basis, not part of the basis itself.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Upper wick length of the evaluated bar: high minus the greater of open and close.
Lower wick length of the evaluated bar: the lesser of open and close, minus low.
Total range of the evaluated bar: high minus low. Denominator of the wick ratio.

terms.label: near resistance
terms.why_unresolved: Two separate things are missing and neither is a threshold. First, resistance is never constructed: the source does not say which swing, over what lookback, on which timeframe, nor whether it is a single price or a zone. Second, 'near' has no reference to be near to until the first is settled, so no tolerance can even be expressed. Swing detection, pivot construction, prior-day levels and volume-profile nodes are materially different constructions that disagree on real data, and choosing between them would be HSA inventing trading semantics the source never stated.

resolution_needed.description: Decide how the resistance level is constructed — the detection method, the lookback, the timeframe, and whether it is a price or a band — and only then the tolerance that counts as 'near'. Both are needed; the tolerance alone is not sufficient.

candidate_definitions.label: Swing high over a fixed lookback, with a tolerance in ATR
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: Resistance is the highest high over a parameterised lookback of N bars on a stated timeframe. Price is near it when the distance from the current close to that level is at most a parameterised multiple of ATR.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Candidate resistance level from swing detection over the stated lookback.
Scale for the proximity tolerance, so the tolerance is instrument- and regime-relative.
Current price used to measure distance to the level.

candidate_definitions.label: Prior-session high, with a tolerance in price units
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: Resistance is the prior session's high on a stated timeframe. Price is near it when the distance from the current close is at most a parameterised number of price units.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Candidate resistance level taken from the previous session.
Current price used to measure distance to the level.

terms.label: strong trend
terms.why_unresolved: 'Trend strength' names no quantity. ADX, moving-average separation, the slope of a regression over a lookback, the count of consecutive higher highs, and net displacement over a window are all defensible readings of the same phrase, and they disagree on real data — they can rank the same two charts in opposite orders. The missing input is therefore the construction itself, not a threshold on an agreed construction. Once a construction is chosen, its cut-off becomes an ordinary bounded parameter.

resolution_needed.description: State which construction of trend strength applies, and on which timeframe: the indicator or computation, its lookback, and the direction rule. The threshold can follow once the construction is fixed.

candidate_definitions.label: ADX above a threshold
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: Trend is strong when ADX over a parameterised period on a stated timeframe is at or above a parameterised threshold.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Directional-movement trend-strength reading over the stated period.

candidate_definitions.label: Moving-average separation and ordering
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: Trend is strong when the fast and slow moving averages are correctly ordered for the direction and their separation, normalised by ATR, is at or above a parameterised threshold.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Fast moving average over the stated period.
Slow moving average over the stated period.
Normaliser so separation is comparable across instruments and regimes.

terms.label: confirmation candle
terms.why_unresolved: Nothing in the phrase says what the candle must do, or what it confirms. Engulfing the prior bar, closing beyond a prior extreme, closing in the top third of its own range, or simply being a second bar in the same direction are all called confirmation candles by working traders, and they are different mechanical tests rather than different settings of one test. The pattern itself is the missing definition, so there is no quantity to threshold.

resolution_needed.description: State the candle pattern that constitutes confirmation, what it is confirming, and on which timeframe it is evaluated. Note that a phrase which names the pattern — for example 'no-wick directional confirmation' — does resolve; 'confirmation candle' alone does not.

candidate_definitions.label: Close beyond the prior bar's extreme
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: The evaluated bar closes beyond the prior bar's high for LONG, or below its low for SHORT, on the stated timeframe.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Close of the evaluated bar.
High of the immediately preceding bar.
Low of the immediately preceding bar.

candidate_definitions.label: Bullish or bearish engulfing
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: The evaluated bar's body fully engulfs the prior bar's body and closes in the trade direction.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Body size and direction of the evaluated bar.
Body size and direction of the immediately preceding bar.

terms.label: good breakout
terms.why_unresolved: The qualifier does not attach to any stated quantity. It could mean closing beyond the level rather than wicking through it, expansion in volume, follow-through on the next bar, or the absence of an immediate return inside the range. Those are different mechanical tests, not different settings of one test, so no single parameter can carry the meaning. The level being broken is frequently undefined as well.

resolution_needed.description: State what distinguishes a qualifying breakout from a non-qualifying one: the level being broken and how it is constructed, whether a close beyond it is required, and any follow-through or volume condition, each with the bar count over which it is measured.

candidate_definitions.label: Close beyond the level, with follow-through
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: The bar closes beyond a stated level, and the next N bars do not close back inside it, where N is a parameterised bar count on the stated timeframe.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Close used to test both the break and the follow-through.
The level being broken, constructed by a stated method.

candidate_definitions.label: Close beyond the level, with volume expansion
candidate_definitions.measurable_definition: The bar closes beyond a stated level and its volume is at least a parameterised multiple of the mean volume over a parameterised lookback.

required_hermes_fields.purpose: Close used to test the break.
Volume of the breaking bar.
Mean volume over the stated lookback, as the comparison base.
